source.title: Noise Injection Node Regularization for Robust Learning
source.authors: N. Levi; I. Bloch; M. Freytsis; T. Volansky

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents reading.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests noise-injection node regularization for robustness and generalization, not whether gradient-based training reaches near-zero classification error under the recipes named in the claim versions. Its training accuracy is used as a stopping condition or mentioned for its own NINR experiments; this does not test the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training accuracy as a stopping condition (98% or 100%) and reports that excessive injected noise degrades accuracy to random guessing. Neither is a test of the claim versions about training error under the listed initialization, depth, learning-rate, or normalization conditions. The corruption, domain-shift, clean-test, and adversarial-robustness results concern a different behavior.
record.test_reason: The study measures NINR robustness and generalization, rather than any listed version. Training-accuracy stopping rules do not establish attained training error. Its catapult dynamics arise from deliberately increasing injected noise at fixed learning rate; it does not test learning rates relative to the initial linearized model's stability limit or track edge-of-stability sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors propose NINR to improve robustness against input perturbations and some domain shifts while generally maintaining clean-data generalization. The strongest corruption-robustness gains occur in the catapult regime, with slower convergence and possible degradation under a fixed training budget.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies Noise Injection Node Regularization and robustness/generalization outcomes, not the training-error mechanisms or conditions specified in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise injection magnitude and phase affect robustness and convergence; architecture, location of noise injection, noise distribution, and optimizer are varied in the robustness experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: NINR improves robustness to random input corruption in tested settings while generally preserving clean-test accuracy; catapult configurations can require longer training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive noise injection can improve corruption robustness, with gains and convergence costs depending on injection magnitude and architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Domain-shift and adversarial-attack performance varies across architectures, regularizers, and attack types.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NINR's benefits under domain shifts and adversarial attacks depend on the tested setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 2.2 and Figure 3 report initial loss growth followed by recovery at large injected-noise magnitudes, and failure to learn at still larger magnitudes. Appendix B analyzes this noise-dependent discrete-time instability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing injected noise at fixed learning rate can produce decay, catapult recovery, or divergence in NINR training.

record.problems: Robustness results are mostly figure-based in the supplied text; several experiments use 10 runs and optimizer/noise-distribution comparisons use 5 runs. The paper describes CIFAR-10 results as preliminary. Its accuracy stopping criteria do not establish the training-error claim under the versions' conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results qualify as rows. The reported robustness and clean-test accuracy metrics address effects of NINR on test behavior, not the named training-error, width/local-minimum, depth, initialization, learning-rate-stability, or batch-normalization claims.

untested.parts: Attained training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random labels, and its dependence on capacity or regularization. The 98% stopping criterion is not a reported attainment result.
Spurious-minimum frequency as teacher/student widths and excess student neurons vary.
Training-error degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts, special initialization, or Fixup.
Effects of activation-matched or orthogonal initialization on training speed and trainable depth.
Recovery above the initial linearized stability limit, curvature reduction during recovery, edge-of-stability training, and divergence below the initial threshold.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and tolerated learning rates, and comparison with normalization-free Fixup training.

record.verdict_notes: The empty row set is appropriate for these versions. Batch normalization and Gaussian initialization are recipe components without relevant comparisons. The paper cites the original catapult and random-label studies but supplies no qualifying test of their listed claims.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sufficiently large convolutional networks reach zero or near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted or random labels; smaller models, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
Whether student width relative to teacher width changes the rate of spurious minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Whether depth raises training error in plain batch-normalized networks and whether identity shortcuts, special initialization, or Fixup prevent that effect.
Whether activation-matched, orthogonal, or convolution-kernel initializations change training speed or trainable depth.
Whether above-stability learning rates yield recovery or edge-of-stability behavior, and when runs diverge.
Whether batch normalization accelerates accuracy gains or increases tolerated learning rates, or Fixup enables normalization-free residual training.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
